facts: A normal distribution is **symmetrical**: the left and right halves are mirror images about the centre.
The mean, median and mode of a normal distribution are all approximately equal and sit at the centre.
Most of the data sits near the centre, and the frequencies decrease steadily towards both **tails**.
A **skewed** display has one longer tail, so it is not normal even though it has a single peak.
A display with two peaks is **bimodal**, and a flat display has no peak; neither shape is normal.
Real data is rarely a perfect bell, so 'approximately normal' is enough when the shape is close.
On two normal curves drawn on the same scale, the curve whose peak is further right has the larger mean.
A wider, flatter curve has the larger standard deviation; a taller, narrower curve has the smaller one.
steps: Check the display is roughly symmetrical
Check there is a single central peak with the frequencies falling away on both sides
Check the mean, median and mode are approximately equal

foundation.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of pages read per day by $80$ students.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Pages} & 12 & 13 & 14 & 15 & 16 & 17 & 18 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 3 & 9 & 17 & 24 & 16 & 8 & 3 \end{array}$
Could this data be normally distributed?
Give reasons.
foundation.solution_text:
The largest frequency is at $15$, and the frequencies fall away on both sides: $17$, $9$, $3$ to the left and $16$, $8$, $3$ to the right.
The two sides are close to mirror images, so the display is approximately symmetrical with a single central peak.
Yes, this data is approximately normally distributed.

The tallest column is at the far left and the columns get steadily shorter to the right.
There is a long tail on the right and no tail on the left, so the display is not symmetrical.
The data is positively skewed rather than bell-shaped, so it is not normally distributed.

foundation.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of vehicles passing a checkpoint in each of $47$ one-minute intervals.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Vehicles} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 9 & 10 & 9 & 10 & 9 \end{array}$
Could this data be normally distributed?
Give reasons.
foundation.solution_text:
The frequencies are all between $9$ and $10$, so the display is flat.
It is symmetrical, but there is no central peak and no tails, so it is not bell-shaped.
No, this data is not normally distributed.

A normal curve is symmetrical about its mean, so the mean is at the peak.
The peak of $Q$ is further to the right than the peak of $P$.
Curve $Q$ has the higher mean.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher records two sets of data:
$\text{Set A}$: the heights of $500$ adult women
$\text{Set B}$: the number of children in each of $500$ families
Which set is more likely to be normally distributed?
Justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Adult heights cluster around a middle value, with fewer women at each extreme and roughly the same number above and below the middle.
Family sizes bunch at the small values $0$, $1$ and $2$ with a tail stretching to the right, so that display is positively skewed.
Set A is more likely to be normally distributed.

development.question_text:
The table shows the number of eggs laid per week by each of $145$ hens.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Eggs} & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 & 10 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 15 & 30 & 43 & 30 & 15 & 6 \end{array}$
Calculate the mean, median and mode, then justify whether this data is approximately normally distributed.
development.solution_text:
$\text{Mean} = \dfrac{4(6)+5(15)+6(30)+7(43)+8(30)+9(15)+10(6)}{145}$
$= \dfrac{1015}{145}$
$= 7$
The $73$rd value is the middle one of $145$, and the running totals are $6$, $21$, $51$, $94$, so the median is $7$.
The largest frequency is $43$, so the mode is $7$.
The mean, median and mode are all $7$, and the frequencies are symmetrical about $7$ with a single central peak, so the data is approximately normally distributed.

There are two tall columns, at $2$ and at $6$, with a dip between them at $4$.
The display is bimodal, so it does not have the single central peak a bell curve has.
The data is not normally distributed.

Curve $S$ is wider and flatter, so its data is more spread out.
Curve $S$ has the larger standard deviation.
Both peaks are at the same place on the horizontal axis, so the two curves have the same mean.

development.question_text:
A teacher records the ages, in whole years, of the $24$ students in her Year $12$ class.
Explain why this data is unlikely to be normally distributed.
development.solution_text:
Nearly every Year $12$ student is $17$, with only a few aged $16$ or $18$.
The display is one tall column with almost nothing either side, so there are no tails falling away steadily.
The shape is not a bell curve, so the ages are unlikely to be normally distributed.

development.question_text:
The table shows the marks out of $36$ scored by $70$ students on a short test.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Mark} & 30 & 31 & 32 & 33 & 34 & 35 & 36 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 & 17 & 25 & 13 \end{array}$
Could this data be normally distributed?
Give reasons.
development.solution_text:
The largest frequency is at $35$, which is near the right-hand end rather than the centre.
The frequencies stretch a long way down to the left ($17$, $8$, $4$, $2$, $1$) but only drop to $13$ on the right, so the tail is on the left.
The display is negatively skewed, not symmetrical, so it is not normally distributed.

mastery.question_text:
The table shows the number of days per week that each of $49$ adults exercised.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Days} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 30 & 6 & 2 & 2 \end{array}$
Riley says, "The mean, median and mode are all $4$, so this data must be normally distributed." Show that Riley's three averages are correct, and explain why his conclusion is wrong.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{Mean} = \dfrac{1(2)+2(3)+3(4)+4(30)+5(6)+6(2)+7(2)}{49}$
$= \dfrac{196}{49}$
$= 4$
The $25$th value is the middle one of $49$, and the running totals are $2$, $5$, $9$, $39$, so the median is $4$.
The largest frequency is $30$, so the mode is $4$.
Equal averages are not enough: the frequencies either side of $4$ are $2$, $3$, $4$ on the left and $6$, $2$, $2$ on the right, so the display is not symmetrical.
The display is also a single sharp spike rather than a bell that falls away gradually, so the data is not normally distributed.

Curve $B$ is the widest and flattest of the three, so its values are the most spread out.
Curve $B$ has the largest standard deviation.
A normal curve is symmetrical about its mean, so the mean sits under the peak.

mastery.question_text:
A large dataset has a mean of $34$, a median of $40$ and a mode of $44$.
Without drawing the data, explain why it cannot be approximately normally distributed.
mastery.solution_text:
For a normal distribution the mean, median and mode are all approximately equal.
Here they are $34$, $40$ and $44$, which differ by $6$ and by $10$, so they are nowhere near equal.
The mean is well below the mode, which happens when a long tail on the left drags the mean down, so the data is skewed rather than symmetrical.
The data cannot be approximately normally distributed.
